title: What is the Java Platform Module System (JPMS, Java 9), what directives does `module-info.java` use (requires/exports/opens/provides/uses), and when is adopting it worth the friction?
shortTitle: What is the Java Platform Module System (JPMS), and what do the module-info.java directives do?
topicTitle: What is the Java Platform Module System

s1_definition.profdef: The Java Platform Module System, introduced in Java 9 under Project Jigsaw, is a language and runtime feature that groups packages into named, self-describing modules with explicit dependencies and explicit public surfaces. A module is declared by a `module-info.java` file at the root of its source tree, and its directives are `requires` (what other modules it depends on), `exports` (which of its packages are visible to other modules at compile and run time), `opens` (which packages are available for deep reflection), `provides ... with` (which service implementations it offers), and `uses` (which service interfaces it consumes). JPMS gives strong encapsulation, reliable configuration checked at startup, and a scalable platform where the JDK itself is split into modules.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India as a secure building. Before JPMS, every department's doors were unlocked — anyone could walk into the vault, the audit room, or HR and grab internal files, as long as they knew the room name. JPMS is like issuing each department a signed charter that says exactly three things: which other departments it is allowed to enter (`requires`), which of its own rooms the public may enter (`exports`), and which rooms the auditors may inspect with a special pass (`opens`). If the payments department says it needs the fraud department but the fraud department does not exist, the building manager refuses to open at all in the morning (startup-time checking) instead of discovering the problem at noon when a customer is waiting.
s1_definition.oneliner: JPMS turns a loose bag of packages into named modules with declared dependencies and an explicit public surface, enforced by the compiler and the JVM.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Java Platform Module System, introduced in Java 9 under Project Jigsaw, is a language and runtime feature that groups packages into named, self-describing modules with explicit dependencies and explicit public surfaces. A module is declared by a `module-info.java` file at the root of its source tree, and its directives are `requires` (what other modules it depends on), `exports` (which of its packages are visible to other modules at compile and run time), `opens` (which packages are available for deep reflection), `provides ... with` (which service implementations it offers), and `uses` (which service interfaces it consumes). JPMS gives strong encapsulation, reliable configuration checked at startup, and a scalable platform where the JDK itself is split into modules.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India as a secure building. Before JPMS, every department's doors were unlocked — anyone could walk into the vault, the audit room, or HR and grab internal files, as long as they knew the room name. JPMS is like issuing each department a signed charter that says exactly three things: which other departments it is allowed to enter (`requires`), which of its own rooms the public may enter (`exports`), and which rooms the auditors may inspect with a special pass (`opens`). If the payments department says it needs the fraud department but the fraud department does not exist, the building manager refuses to open at all in the morning (startup-time checking) instead of discovering the problem at noon when a customer is waiting.

**One line to remember:** JPMS turns a loose bag of packages into named modules with declared dependencies and an explicit public surface, enforced by the compiler and the JVM.

sections.s2_technical:
Before Java 9 the unit of deployment was the JAR, and the classpath was a flat, unordered list. Any public class in any JAR could be used by any other code, so "public" effectively meant "public to the entire world." There was no way to say "this package is my internal implementation, do not touch it." There was also the fragile-classpath problem: missing JARs were discovered lazily as `NoClassDefFoundError` deep into execution, and duplicate or conflicting versions silently shadowed each other. JPMS addresses both by adding a layer above packages called the module.

A module is described by `module-info.java`, which compiles to a `module-info.class`. The `requires` directive names a dependency, for example `requires com.bank.audit;`. A special form `requires transitive com.bank.audit;` means that any module reading mine automatically also reads audit — this is how you re-export an API you expose in your own method signatures. `requires static` means the dependency is needed at compile time but optional at run time, useful for annotations.

The `exports` directive makes a package part of the public API, for example `exports com.bank.payments.api;`. Packages you do not export are strongly encapsulated — even their public classes are invisible to other modules, which is the headline feature. A qualified export, `exports com.bank.payments.internal to com.bank.reporting;`, reveals a package to named modules only, useful for friend-style access between cooperating modules.

The `opens` directive is about reflection. Under JPMS, reflective access that calls `setAccessible(true)` on members of another module fails unless that package is opened. `opens com.bank.model;` allows deep reflection into that package at run time, which frameworks like Hibernate, Jackson, and Spring need to read private fields. You can open to specific modules with `opens com.bank.model to com.fasterxml.jackson.databind;`, or make the whole module open with `open module com.bank.app { ... }`.

The service directives wire up the `ServiceLoader` mechanism. A provider module writes `provides com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator with com.bank.spi.impl.GstFeeCalculator;`, and a consumer module writes `uses com.bank.spi.FeeCalculator;`. This replaces the old `META-INF/services` text files with a compiler-checked declaration.

At startup the module system resolves the module graph: it reads every module's descriptor, verifies that all `requires` are satisfiable, and checks that no two readable modules export the same package to the same module (the split-package rule). If anything is wrong, the JVM refuses to start, turning a run-time surprise into a launch-time error. The JDK itself ships as about ninety platform modules; `java.base` is the always-present core, and tools like `jlink` can build a trimmed custom runtime containing only the modules your application requires, which shrinks containers dramatically.

A senior nuance on when adoption is worth the friction: JPMS pays off most for libraries and platforms that want to publish a small, enforced public API and hide internals, and for applications that want small `jlink` runtimes or rely on `ServiceLoader` plugins. The friction is real — reflective frameworks force many `opens`, some older libraries are not modular and must live as automatic modules, and the split-package rule can break assemblies that worked on the classpath. For a typical Spring Boot microservice that runs fat-JAR on the classpath, the cost usually outweighs the benefit, so many teams stay on the classpath and adopt JPMS selectively for shared libraries.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has a payments library used by many internal teams. The library has a clean public API in one package and a messy internal package full of helper classes. On the old classpath, other teams discovered the internal helper classes and started calling them directly. When the library team tried to refactor the internals, half the bank broke. This is exactly the problem strong encapsulation solves: with JPMS we `exports` only the API package and keep the internal package private to the module, so no other team can even see the helpers, and we are free to refactor them.

Problem 2 — The reporting team legitimately needs one internal class from payments, but no one else should. On the classpath there was no way to say "only reporting may use this." This is exactly what a qualified export does: `exports com.bank.payments.internal to com.bank.reporting;` reveals that package to the reporting module alone.

Problem 3 — Jackson needs to read the private fields of our money transfer model to serialize it to JSON, but strong encapsulation blocks reflection by default. This is what `opens` solves: we open the model package so the framework can reflect, while keeping normal code still unable to call our internals.

The mini-project is two modules. The `com.bank.payments` module exports its public API, keeps an internal package encapsulated, qualifies one export to reporting, and opens its model package for reflection. The `com.bank.app` module requires payments and calls only the public API. The runnable demo shows a transfer for Rajesh and demonstrates that the public API works while the internal package is invisible.

The code contains: `module-info.java` for the payments module; a public `TransferService` API; an encapsulated internal validator; a model class; and a consuming application module with its own `module-info.java`.

```
payments-platform/
├── payments/
│   ├── module-info.java
│   └── com/bank/payments/
│       ├── api/
│       │   └── TransferService.java        (exported public API)
│       ├── internal/
│       │   └── TransferValidator.java      (encapsulated, NOT exported)
│       └── model/
│           └── Account.java                (opened for reflection)
├── app/
│   ├── module-info.java
│   └── com/bank/app/
│       └── PaymentsApp.java                (consumes the public API only)
└── util/
    └── BankLogFormatter.java
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile both modules into a module output directory
javac -d out --module-source-path . $(find . -name "*.java")

# Run the application module, naming the main class
java --module-path out --module com.bank.app/com.bank.app.PaymentsApp

# Build a tiny custom runtime containing ONLY the modules we need
jlink --module-path out:$JAVA_HOME/jmods \
      --add-modules com.bank.app \
      --output custom-runtime
./custom-runtime/bin/java --module com.bank.app/com.bank.app.PaymentsApp
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a request to transfer Rs.50000 from Rajesh (SAV2001, balance Rs.1000000) to Priya (CUR3001, balance Rs.250000).

Step 1: At JVM startup, the module system reads `com.bank.app`'s descriptor, sees `requires com.bank.payments`, and resolves the graph. It verifies payments exists and exports the packages app will touch. If payments were missing, the JVM would refuse to start right here — the data journey would never begin.

Step 2: `PaymentsApp.main` creates two `Account` objects. These live in `com.bank.payments.model`, which is opened and exported, so app can construct and read them freely.

Step 3: App creates a `TransferService` from the exported `api` package. This is allowed because payments `exports com.bank.payments.api`.

Step 4: Inside `transfer`, the service calls its own `TransferValidator`, which lives in the encapsulated `internal` package. This call is legal because both classes are in the same module — encapsulation is between modules, not within one.

Step 5: The validator confirms the amount is positive and Rajesh has enough balance. Rajesh is debited from Rs.1000000 to Rs.950000, Priya is credited from Rs.250000 to Rs.300000.

Step 6: The service logs success. Back in app, the final balances are logged. At no point could app reach into the internal validator, because the module boundary hides it.

```
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:00 PM com.bank.payments.api.TransferService transfer
INFO: Transfer Rs.50000.00 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 SUCCESS
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:00 PM com.bank.app.PaymentsApp main
INFO: Rajesh balance: Rs.950000.00
Oct 26, 2026 3:46:00 PM com.bank.app.PaymentsApp main
INFO: Priya  balance: Rs.300000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Startup: JVM resolves module graph
    │  com.bank.app  requires  com.bank.payments  ✓
    │  payments exports: api, model(open)   NOT: internal
    ▼
  PaymentsApp.main (module com.bank.app)
    │ new Account("SAV2001", Rajesh, 1,000,000)   ← model package (exported)
    │ new Account("CUR3001", Priya,   250,000)
    │ new TransferService()                        ← api package (exported)
    ▼
  TransferService.transfer(rajesh, priya, 50000)   (module com.bank.payments)
    │ validator.validate(...)                       ← internal package (same module OK)
    │ rajesh.debit(50000)   1,000,000 → 950,000
    │ priya.credit(50000)     250,000 → 300,000
    ▼
  Back in app:
    │ app CANNOT touch com.bank.payments.internal  ✗ (encapsulated)
    ▼
  Output: SAV2001 = Rs.950000, CUR3001 = Rs.300000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Java Platform Module System, added in Java 9 under Project Jigsaw, is a layer above packages that groups them into named modules, each described by a module-info file. A module declares what it depends on with the requires directive, what packages it makes public with the exports directive, which packages are open for deep reflection with the opens directive, and how it participates in the service loader mechanism with the provides and uses directives. The two big wins are strong encapsulation, meaning a public class in a non-exported package is simply invisible to other modules, and reliable configuration, meaning the module graph is resolved and validated at startup so a missing or conflicting dependency fails the launch instead of failing hours later in production.

In my banking work the problem that modules solve directly was a shared payments library at National Bank of India. On the old classpath, other teams reached into our internal helper classes because public meant public to everyone, and when we tried to refactor those helpers the whole bank broke. With modules we export only the api package that holds the transfer service, we keep the internal validator package encapsulated so nobody outside can even see it, and we are finally free to refactor internals safely. When the reporting team genuinely needed one internal class, I used a qualified export that reveals that package to the reporting module alone, and when Jackson needed to serialize our account model I used opens on just the model package so the framework can reflect while ordinary code still cannot touch our internals.

I am also honest about the friction, because that is what a senior engineer weighs. Reflective frameworks force you to open many packages, some older libraries are not modular and have to be treated as automatic modules, and the split-package rule can break assemblies that worked fine on the classpath. So I adopt modules deliberately. For a shared library or platform where I want a small enforced public surface and a trimmed jlink runtime, modules are clearly worth it. For an ordinary Spring Boot microservice that runs as a fat jar on the classpath, the cost usually outweighs the benefit, so I stay on the classpath there. The principle I carry is least privilege: expose the smallest surface that the consumers truly need, and hide everything else behind the module boundary.
